facts.value: The judiciary is the system of courts that applies the law and contracts. Under the doctrine of the separation of powers, the judiciary generally does not make statutory law (which is the responsibility of the legislature) or enforce law (which is the responsibility of the executive), but rather interprets, defends, and applies the law to the facts of each case.
facts.programme_association: Law, Human Rights in Criminal Justice - LLM or MA

facts.value: However, in some countries the judiciary does make common law.
facts.programme_association: Law, Human Rights in Criminal Justice - LLM or MA

facts.value: In many jurisdictions the judicial branch has the power of judicial interpretation, judicial review and constitutional review.
facts.programme_association: Law, Human Rights in Criminal Justice - LLM or MA

facts.value: Courts with judicial review power may annul the laws and rules of the state when it finds them incompatible with other laws, such as primary legislation, constitution, treaties or international law.
facts.programme_association: Law, Human Rights in Criminal Justice - LLM or MA

facts.value: The judiciary can also be thought of as a nonviolent mechanism for conflict resolution.
facts.programme_association: Law, Human Rights in Criminal Justice - LLM or MA

facts.value: Political bias, sentencing disparities, and higher leniency than the public reduce the political legitimacy of the judiciary.
facts.programme_association: Law, Human Rights in Criminal Justice - LLM or MA

facts.value: Public confidence in the judiciary varies by country according to opinion polls.
